<reason>An exceptionally close debate between two polished cases: B's form-vs-invoice taxonomy ("Keep the form. Cut the invoice.") was elegant and its elopement reductio was real pressure, while A's sociological account of expectation-as-enforced tracked the motion's premise better. A edged it by controlling the late clash: its two pressure questions were genuine traps, and though B answered them directly and well (kin-facing ceremony as the costly duty; the "sting" as enforcement), A converted those answers into a concession narrative B never fully escaped — the obligation B saved was justified by function (A's "earned, not inherited" standard), and the enforcement B licensed was the same disapproval that inflates weddings, capped only by assertion ("the form is the cap"). A also met B's strongest point head-on with the promise-vs-performance fork on elopement rather than dodging. B's narrowing of "traditional expectations" to the minimal rite increasingly conceded the motion's practical core, leaving B defending a cheap obligation the motion's "little, not none" wording largely absorbs.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2: embracing the elopement and forking B — "Either the promise is the thing or the performance is. They cannot claim the first while policing the second" — then, in the closing, turning B's direct A1/A2 answers (function-justified duty, the uncappable "sting") into the decisive concession narrative.</best_rebuttal>
